title: Range Partitioning — Core Method
description: Range partitioning splits an index by key intervals — A–F, G–M, and so on — so each partition holds a contiguous slice of the key space. Lookups for a specific key go straight to the owning partition, and range queries touch only the partitions their interval overlaps. The risk is skew: real data clusters, leaving some partitions hot and others empty, which is fixed by splitting hot ranges. Range partitioning is the natural choice when queries are key- or range-oriented. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Hash Partitioning — Core Method
description: Hash partitioning spreads keys uniformly by hashing the key and taking the remainder modulo the partition count, which eliminates skew no matter how the data clusters. The price is locality: range queries must fan out to every partition, because adjacent keys land in different places. Adding partitions rehashes everything unless consistent hashing is used. Hash partitioning wins whenever the workload is point lookups and even load matters most. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Partition Pruning — Core Method
description: A partitioned index only pays off if queries skip irrelevant partitions: pruning uses the query's predicates against partition metadata — key ranges, bloom filters, min/max statistics — to eliminate partitions that cannot match. Effective pruning turns a hundred-partition fan-out into a two-partition lookup. The engine logs prune rates per query shape, which reveals when partition boundaries no longer fit the workload. Pruning is where partitioning earns its keep. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
PARTS = [{"range": ("a", "g"), "n": 100}, {"range": ("g", "p"), "n": 150}, {"range": ("p", "z"), "n": 90}]
def prune(lo, hi):
    return [i for i, p in enumerate(PARTS) if not (hi < p["range"][0] or lo > p["range"][1])]
print("query [h,m] touches partitions:", prune("h", "m"))

title: Global Result Merge — Core Method
description: Queries that span partitions get partial ranked lists back from each one, and the global merge combines them into a single correct ranking. For top-k queries each partition returns its local top-k, and the merger's k-way merge keeps the global order without re-sorting everything. Scores must be comparable across partitions, which is guaranteed by using the same scoring function everywhere. Correct merging is what makes a partitioned index behave like one big index. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import heapq
p1 = [(0.9, "d1"), (0.4, "d2")]
p2 = [(0.8, "d3"), (0.7, "d4")]
merged = heapq.nlargest(3, p1 + p2)
for s, d in merged: print("%s %.1f" % (d, s))

title: Rebalance Simulation — Core Method
description: Data grows unevenly, so partitions drift out of balance; the rebalancer simulates moves — splitting hot partitions, merging cold ones — and scores each plan by resulting balance versus data moved. Only plans that beat a threshold execute, because moving data is itself expensive. Simulations run on partition statistics, not raw data, so thousands of plans can be tried cheaply. Planned rebalancing keeps the cluster even without surprise migrations. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
sizes = [100, 100, 400, 100]
avg = sum(sizes) / len(sizes)
worst = max(sizes)
print("max/avg imbalance: %.2f" % (worst / avg))
print("action:", "split partition 2" if worst / avg > 1.5 else "balanced")
